To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the 1986–87 NIDR survey revealed a decrease in carious lesions in all tooth surface categories compared to the 1979–80 survey.
there was an overall decrease in the caries attack rate for the primary and permanent dentitions during the 1976-87 period.
the 1986/87 survey showed a 35% decrease in the prevalence of caries on all tooth surfaces compared to the 1979/80 survey.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the study of tooth surface-specific caries patterns in the US school-aged population, and the changes in these patterns between two National Surveys conducted by the National Institute of Dental and Craniofacial Research (NIDCR) in 1979-80 and 1986-87.
the study of tooth surface-specific dental caries attack patterns in the United States and the relationship of these patterns to caries prevalence.
the analysis of the dental caries patterns in the primary and permanent teeth of US schoolchildren.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the 1986 survey found fewer tooth surfaces with caries than the 1979 survey for all surfaces and for all teeth.
the overall decrease in caries was greatest for pit and fissures, followed in decreasing order by posterior approximal surfaces, all other smooth surfaces and primary incisors.
the 1986 National Survey of Dental Caries in US Children found that caries prevalence decreased in all age groups and all tooth surfaces, with the exception of primary incisors.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there was a significant reduction in the proportion of all tooth surfaces attacked by dental caries in both the primary and the permanent dentition during the 1970-1980 and 1986-87 periods.
the overall decrease in dental caries prevalence in the US school-aged children was 31% during the 7-year period between the 1979 and 1987 NIDR surveys.

there were statistically significant differences in the proportions of tooth surfaces attacked in 1986-87 compared with those attacked in 1979-80, and that the differences were larger in the permanent than in the primary dentition.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the overall caries attack pattern has been shifting from the primary dentition to the permanent dentition and from smooth to non-smooth surfaces during the 1970s and 1980s.
there has been a decrease in dental caries prevalence for both the primary and permanent dentitions in the United States over the last 8 years.
there was an overall decline in the prevalence of caries among schoolchildren during the 1986–87 survey, and that this decline was more marked for permanent than for primary tooth surfaces.
